Q: typing.Any vs object? A:

Any and object are superficially similar, but in fact are entirely opposite in meaning.

object is the root of Python's metaclass hierarchy. Every single class inherits from object. That means that object is in a certain sense the most restrictive type you can give values. If you have a value of type object, the only methods you are permitted to call are ones that are a part of every single object. For example:

foo: object = 3

# Error, not all objects have a method 'hello'
bar = foo.hello()   

# OK, all objects have a __str__ method
print(str(foo))

In contrast, Any is an escape hatch meant to allow you to mix together dynamic and statically typed code. Any is the least restrictive type -- any possible method or operation is permitted on a value of type Any. For example:

from typing import Any
foo: Any = 3

# OK, foo could be any type, and that type might have a 'hello' method
# Since we have no idea what hello() is, `bar` will also have a type of Any
bar = foo.hello()

# Ok, for similar reasons
print(str(foo))

You should generally try and use Any only for cases where...

  1. As a way of mixing together dynamic and statically typed code. For example, if you have many dynamic and complex functions, and don't have time to fully statically type all of them, you could settle for just giving them a return type of Any to nominally bring them into the typechecked work. (Or to put it another way, Any is a useful tool for helping migrate an untypechecked codebase to a typed codebase in stages).
  2. As a way of giving a type to an expression that is difficult to type. For example, Python's type annotations currently do not support recursive types, which makes typing things like arbitrary JSON dicts difficult. As a temporary measure, you might want to give your JSON dicts a type of Dict[str, Any], which is a bit better then nothing.

In contrast, use object for cases where you want to indicate in a typesafe way that a value MUST literally work with any possible object in existence.

My recommendation is to avoid using Any except in cases where there is no alternative. Any is a concession -- a mechanism for allowing dynamism where we'd really rather live in a typesafe world.

For more information, see:

  • https://docs.python.org/3/library/typing.html#the-any-type
  • http://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/kinds_of_types.html#the-any-type

For your particular example, I would use TypeVars, rather then either object or Any. What you want to do is to indicate that you want to return the type of whatever is contained within the list. If the list will always contain the same type (which is typically the case), you would want to do:

from typing import List, TypeVar

T = TypeVar('T')
def get_item(L: List[T], i: int) -> T:
    return L[i]

This way, your get_item function will return the most precise type as possible.

Q: @sidebase/nuxt-auth throwing '404 Page not found: /session' error A:

Ah, I ran into this exact issue before. The reason you’re seeing:

[GET] "/session": 404 Page not found: /session
Recursion detected at /session

is because @sidebase/nuxt-auth is trying to reach the session endpoint at the wrong path. By default, Nuxt Auth expects all auth routes to live under /api/auth, so your session endpoint should actually be /api/auth/session—not just /session.

The main problem in your config is that baseURL isn’t set correctly, so the module falls back to the default and ends up pointing at /session. Setting originEnvKey alone doesn’t fix this, because that just tells Nuxt what the domain is; it doesn’t change the endpoint path.

Here’s a straightforward fix:

export default defineNuxtConfig({
  modules: ['@sidebase/nuxt-auth'],

  auth: {
    provider: { type: 'authjs' },
    secret: process.env.NUXT_AUTH_SECRET,
    baseURL: '/api/auth' // this ensures /session points correctly
  }
})

And in your .env:

NUXT_AUTH_SECRET=super-secret

A couple of things to double-check:

Make sure you actually have the handler file in your project:

server/api/auth/[...].ts

If it’s missing, /api/auth/session will always 404.

You can remove NUXT_AUTH_ORIGIN for local development unless you need cross-domain auth.

Once you set baseURL correctly and have the handler in place, the 404 and recursion warnings should disappear, and /api/auth/session will work as expected.

Q: How to correctly set PYTHONPATH for Visual Studio Code A:

The documentation is missing some important details.

Example

Suppose your project layout is like this

myproject/
    .vscode/
        settings.json
    .env
    src/
        a_module.py
    tests/
        test_a.py

Open the settings.json file and insert these lines

// On linux use "terminal.integrated.env.linux": {
"terminal.integrated.env.windows": {
    "PYTHONPATH": "${workspaceFolder}/src;${workspaceFolder}/tests"
},
// The next line can be omitted, unless you've modified the global default
"python.envFile": "${workspaceFolder}/.env",

Note that ${workspaceFolder} evaluates to myproject, it is not to the .vscode folder.

In the .env file enter this

PYTHONPATH=src;test
# Paths are relative to the workspace folder, so above is equivalent to
# WORKSPACE_FOLDER=C:/full/path/to/myproject
# PYTHONPATH=${WORKSPACE_FOLDER}/src;${WORKSPACE_FOLDER}/tests

Note that on all platforms, including Windows, the slashes in the path lean forward, like so /. Different paths are separated with a ; on Windows, on other platforms with a :.

Final step, restart VS Code.

This blog was helpful.

Q: How can I use a browser's Inspect feature to fix someone else's bug? A:

You have two options:

  • Contact admin of page via mail, and inform them about that

  • or use a userscript (Tampermonkey/Greasemonkey/whatever) that intercepts the broken link and performs the fetch/ajax request shown in the page. That avoids editing the site and runs locally on each load.

Q: Python: Can't display images in Zelle graphics.py, tkinter can't read image data A:

To transform your presumed .gif into a reliable GIF, readable by "graphics.py" (Tkinter is what really is behind) or to convert from other formats (e.g. .jpg, etc), you can use:

macOS
sips -s format gif your-source-image.gif --out your-image.gif

Linux
convert your-source-image.gif your-image.gif

Windows (Powershell)
magick your-source-image.gif your-image.gif

This should be enough for the GIF part.

The JPG issue (macOS proceeding; logic valid for other platforms)
If you want your program to work with formats like .jpg leaning on graphics.py (Zelle's book ad hoc graphics library [wrapper]), you will need to install pillow. Apart from the standard brew install pillow, you can go for the local-installation/sandboxed choice (to avoid conflicts with your current Homebrew/native Python installation).
If you try: python3 -m pip install pillow, "error: externally-managed-environment" message will be triggered and you will be advised to do:

  1. python3 -m venv venv                Creates folder on working directory for the isolated environment
  2. source venv/bin/activate        Sources environment configuration
  3. pip install pillow                    Install pillow in the venv folder
  4. python3 your-script.py            Now your script should work properly

This will create an isolated environment apart from your system's Python wide installation. Usually with shell prompt prefixed with: (venv) .... The only drawback is that you will need to source it again anytime you need it.

(or the not recommended although nor dramatic alternative: python3 -m pip install pillow --break-system-packages. Worst case you would need to re-install Python again if relevant-for-you conflicts, arise in the future with related packages)

If after installing pillow you still get: _tkinter.TclError: couldn't recognize data in image file "your-image.jpg", you probably need to tune graphics.py to import and use pillow functionalities (basically to deal with image formats [beyond Tkinter's .gif, .pgm, .ppm, .png] that pillow is capable and "graphics.py" (Tkinter) is not). Later versions of graphics.py should include pillow's awareness. If not, tuning is possible and could require an import... and a couple of lines more in certain places inside graphics.py.

*Zelle's book is for you to learn Object-Oriented Programming, not for you to fight with macOS (or others) graphics drivers and Tkinter dependencies.
